text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

An index prepared by Westpac Banking Corp and the Melbourne Institute of Applied Economic and Social Research rose four per cent during January. The index, the main measure of consumer confidence in Australia, offsets a fall of seven per cent during Deceber which accompanied reports of poor performances from most retailers over Christmas. Page 3.

Australian Conservation Foundation spokesman Mike Krockenberger said last night the ACF was extremely disappointed in the Federal Government's cut in funding from A$187,000 to A$110,000 for 1996-97. The cuts, announced by Federal Environment Minister Robrt Hill, accompanied a retention of total funding for voluntary conservation groups at around the same level as the former Labor Government. Page 3.

Western Australia Premier Richard Court says Australia must develop a taxation regime comparable to those in Singapore or Hong Kong if it wishes to remain competitive into the next century. Court says Australia's comparatively narrow, income-based system is putting pressure on spending programs in health, housing, aged services and higher education. Page 3.

The Queensland Government may be in more trouble over the native title issue as a senior Government source indicated the Government did not obtain formal, written Crown Law advice when it decided to freeze dealings on most leasehold property in the State.Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

In controversial remarks expected to upset the academia, Rod West, the chairman of the Federal Government's new higher education review committee, said yesterday universities should not offer vocational courses such as Diplomas of Education, but should intead concentrate on "creative thinking" and "inspirational teaching". West will head the seven-person committee which has been given a wide brief to draw up a blueprint for the A$5 billion higher education sector over the next two decades. Page 1.

Acting Prime Minister Tim Fischer yesterday hardened his stance on native title by pointing out Parliament's supremacy over the High Court and problems with its Wik decision. Fischer said the Federal Government and Parliament had certain responsibilitiesand obligations apart from what the High Court may determine. Page 1.

Analyst and business forecaster Phil Ruthven says there are a number of trends in the lifestyle of Australians that could cause trouble for retailers. The social and demographic changes in the Australian consumer leaves it almost unrecognisable from a deade or so ago, with spending patterns changing and many businesses struggling as a result. Page 3.

Federal Liberal backbencher and chairman of the parliamentary committee into the National Crime Authority, John Bradford, said yesterday the Federal Government's fight against illegal drugs had little co-ordination and urgency. Bradford's comments followa report by the Australian Bureau of Criminal Intelligence that shows a rise in drug use despite huge increases in arrests for drug-related crimes. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

A peace deal between Kerry Packer and Rupert Murdoch is imminent, as negotiators for News Corporation and the Nine Network thrash out a deal for the television rights to Super League. An announcement, expected tomorrow, should see Nine get the rights to televise Monday Night football. Page 1.

In a move to make Asia the top of the international agenda for 1997, Prime Minister John Howard is planning a diplomatic trip through key Asian capitals in April that aims to boost Australia's regional interests, including a bid for a A$3 billion defence eal with Malaysia that has run into trouble. Page 1.

The Department of Employment, Education, Training and Youth Affairs has warned the results of recent surveys conducted by the Department do not foreshadow any improvement in job growth in the near future, and there are indications of low consumer sentimen and a decline in housing finance commitments that have reinforced the bleak outlook for the economy. Page 3.

As the New South Wales Government awaits the report from a review of the school starting age for children, children entering kindergarten this year will be monitored, following concerns that children would turn six in the year they begin school. A proposal that would copy the current system in Victoria would see children born in May, June and July having to start school in the year they turned six rather than five. Page 3.
THE AGE

As Victorian students await Monday's first round of enrolment offers, State universities look set to reject more school leavers with low TERs in an attempt to shore up their entrance scores and protect their reputation. To fill the void, course quotas are likely to be filled by more adults and non school leavers. The drop in numbers comes in the face of the Howard Government's reduced funding to higher education. Page A1.

In the aftermath of the successful rescue of two yachtsmen from off the coast of Western Australia, Melbourne will lose its role in aviation rescue after allegations of bungling the rescue of one of the men, Thierry Dubois. All sea and land operations are to be co-ordinated from Canberra under the name of the Australian Maritime Safety Authority. Page A2.

Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett has left open the possibility of more privately operated hospital emergency departments if hospital networks could not provide enough doctors for 24-hour emergency care. Page A3.

After protests surrounding the environmental impact of an oil terminal at Crib Point, Shell International has backed down and deferred the project "indefinitely". The company's environmental adviser Dr Peter Langcake said Shell will hold off building the erminal for as long as strong opposition remains. Page A3.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Australian Bureau of Statistics figures released yesterday showed a surprise slump in refinancing for housing of 15 per cent. The figures have shocked building material firms and the construction industry, despite the drop being caused by a reduction in the umber of borrowers switching between lenders. There was also a three per cent fall in the total number of new home loans approved. Page 1.

Optus Vision New South Wales director Rob Hines said yesterday Optus Vision had fallen short of its roll out targets, six months after the launch of its aggressive "New Deal" for cheap local calls. Hines said delivering on the deal was more sophisticatedand technical than originally thought. Page 1.

Australian mining group Queensland Metals Corp has signed an agreement with United States car manufacturer Ford to develop a magnesium metal smelter worth around A$700 million. It is expected Ford will commit more than A$35 million to a large demonstratin plant at QMC's Gladstone operation before developing a commercial smelter on the same site. Page 1.

Industry executives said yesterday Kerry Packer and Rupert Murdoch have begun peace talks to end a year-long dispute over the control of key media and entertainment assets. Packer's Nine Network looks set to purchase the free-to-air television rights to urdoch's Super League as part of a broader deal involving issues such as pay-TV and the supply of Murdoch's Fox film and TV into Australia from the United States. Page 15.

Following Kerry Packer's decision to take a A$342 million stake in Sydney Harbour Casino in the past week, Australia's gaming industry is in turmoil, with fears of imminent closure of the Christmas Island casino and further dissent from unit holders in Townsville's Breakwater Island casino. Page 15.

Housing finance figures for November have shown the first signs of a turnaround in the housing industry as a result of dropped interest rates and a competitive home lending market. For some players in the industry, the figures signal a marked recovery frm the middle of the year, yet Australia's major building products groups expect profits for the next six months to be hampered by a depressed housing market. Page 15.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Australia's share market hit a record yesterday following the unstoppable progress of Wall Street towards the 7000 mark. Australia's all ordinaries index closed at 2438.2, up 18.8 points and ahead of its previous record of 2424.6 reached on December 31 lst year. BHP and other blue-chip resources stocks, as well as the banking sector enjoyed strong gains, as another fall in the gold sector was caused by a further drop in gold prices. Page 21.

With the completion of its aerial cable rollout in the biggest market of Sydney, Optus Vision is now planning a strong push into regional Australia and the country's first pay-per-view broadcast on February 3 - the World Boxing Council heavyweight title fght. The broadcast will cost consumers A$29.95. Page 21.

Wallis inquiry chairman Stan Wallis was at odds with both the banking industry and the Reserve Bank of Australia, as he dismissed the banks' blanket opposition to deposit protection insurance and was then indirectly criticised by the RBA for exposing Austalia's key regulators to allegations of political interference through the Department of Treasury. Page 21.

ANZ Bank chairman Charles Goode yesterday suggested the Wallis inquiry into financial services could result in banking charges being determined more by market forces. Goode told shareholders at the annual meeting in Melbourne that predicted lending growth and higher fee income would offset a further narrowing of the bank's interest margins. Page 23.

Sons of Gwalia Ltd and Dragon Mining NL yesterday enjoyed a rise in their share price following the announcement that both companies have struck what looks to be a large, low-grade nickel deposit near Meekatharra in Western Australia. Sons of Gwalia alsoannounced good results from its Cornishman gold exploration venture with Troy Resources NL at Southern Cross in Western Australia. Page 23.

Santos Ltd's strong exploration focus in the Cooper-Eromanga basins is giving the company pleasing results, with news yesterday of a gas field discovery in the South Australian section of the basins. The Adelaide-based company announced news of the find t the Nephrite-1 exploration well, which follows news of the successful Judga-North 1 well in the Queensland section of the basins. Page 23.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

The Australian All Ordinaries index jumped 18.8 points to 2438.2 yesterday, breaking its previous record set on December 31. The rise was due to strong leading stocks and followed the United States' Dow Jones Industrial Average gaining 53.1 to 6762.3, th London FT-100 covering new ground and highs reached in Paris and nearly New Zealand. Page 25.

At yesterday's annual general meeting, the ANZ Bank outlined a year of cost-cutting, higher fee income and improved lending volumes to compensate for a strong decline in interest margins and to ensure earnings growth in its core domestic markets. The Bank's restructuring program, which has already seen 3,000 jobs go and 61 branches closed, has been heavily criticised by the Finance Sector Union. Page 25.

As rumours circulated that pay TV group Optus Vision had reached settlement with the Seven Network over a court battle that was set to be held in February, and threatened to hold up the A$1 billion-plus float of Optus Communications, Mayne Nickless shares jumped 15 cents to A$8 yesterday. Mayne Nickless has a 25 per cent shareholding in Optus Communications. Page 25.

A survey by Trowbridge Consulting and commissioned by the Australian Investment Managers' Association, Investment Funds Association of Australia and Life, Investment and Superannuation Association of Australia has found institutions could save around A$55 million each year in compliance costs if the number of regulators was cut from four to one. Page 25.

Amid rumours over the possible deal on BHP's shareholding in Foster's Brewing Group, Foster's yesterday successfully gained control of Victorian-based Ballarat Brewing Company . The rival bidder for Ballarat, Guinness Peat Group, gave control to Foster's subsidiary Carlton and United Breweries by accepting a revised offer of A$2.56 a share. Page 27.

Former managing director of the Bisley Investment Corporation, John Corner, yesterday pleaded guilty in the District Court to three Companies Code charges. Corner's plea, changed yesterday after Crown prosecutor Michael Adams, QC, finished opening his cae, brings to an end the eight-year saga following the collapse of the Spedley Group. Page 27.
THE AGE

With the Wallis inquiry expected to recommend the removal of the "six-pillars" policy preventing mergers between the four big banks, ANZ Bank chairman Charles Goode told the bank's annual meeting in Melbourne yesterday that ANZ was not looking to take ove another bank and performance was the key to maintaining its own independence. Page B1.

Canada's Placer Dome has made a world record takeover bid of A$6.4 billion for Bre-X Minerals, the Canadian miner that became an overnight sensation with the discovery of the huge Busang gold resource in Kalimantan, Indonesia. Placer is offering to finane the 57 million ounce gold resource's US$1.7 billion development for annual production from 1999 of some three to four million ounces of gold a year. Page B1.

Foster's Brewing has won control of Ballarat Brewing after raising its offer by six cents to A$2.56 a share on Monday. Rival bidder Guinness Peat Group accepted the revised offer yesterday and Ballarat's independent directors recommended to shareholders hat they also accept the offer. Page B1.

Pasminco's share price rose by 9.2 per cent yesterday to A$2.24, signalling the share market's approval of its deal with RTZ-CRA to buy the Century Zinc project and the nearby Dugald River deposit. If a deal with local Aborigines allows the deal to go ahad, Pasminco's resource base would be more than tripled to 24 million tonnes of zinc. Page B1.

With Qantas' shares rising 13 per cent in the past eight days from A$2.06 to A$2.38, the airline was unable to give the Australian Stock Exchange any explanation for the unusual upsurge. However, analysts said Qantas stock had been undervalued for some time and the airline had improved its performance. Page B1.

Blaming casinos and gambling for much of the Sizzler restaurants' declining sales, the owner of half of the restaurant chain, Jardine Matheson group chairman Robert Sutton, has put the chain on the market. Sutton said negotiations were under way with sevral parties for the sale of the restaurants, including the other major operator of Australian Sizzlers, Collins Food International. Page B2.
